name: Dominica
meta_description: Investigative consulting for matters touching Dominica: CBI-linked due diligence, corporate records, asset tracing and coordinated local inquiries from Nashville.
hero_lede: Matters touching Dominica often centre on citizenship-by-investment holders, small locally registered companies and offshore-style structures. Investigative consulting here means working within a common law system, records that are rarely public, no comprehensive data protection statute and a small, closely connected business community.
intro: Dominica is a small English-speaking island state in the Eastern Caribbean with a population of about 66,000. It is a member of the Organisation of Eastern Caribbean States, uses the East Caribbean dollar issued by the Eastern Caribbean Central Bank, and shares the Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court with its neighbours. Its law follows the English common law tradition. Company records are held by the Companies and Intellectual Property Office in Roseau. As of early 2025 the country had not enacted a comprehensive data protection law. Because the commercial community is small and personal networks are dense, discreet handling of inquiries is as important as the legal framework.

Organisations most often commission work involving Dominica because of its Citizenship by Investment programme, which has made Dominican passports common among internationally mobile individuals. Lenders, counterparties, compliance teams and litigants regularly need to understand the background, source of wealth and true connections of such individuals. Other exposures include real estate and hotel developments marketed to CBI investors, legacy entities from the former international business companies regime, which was repealed in 2021, and contract and supplier disputes linked to post-hurricane reconstruction. Matters usually involve parties outside the island, and the records that matter are often held in several jurisdictions.
legal_system: Dominica has a common law system based on English law, alongside its own statutes. Civil and commercial claims go to the High Court of the Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court sitting in Roseau, and appeals go to the Court of Appeal, which serves the OECS member states. Since March 2015 Dominica's final appellate court has been the Caribbean Court of Justice, which replaced the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council. We have not identified a dedicated domestic commercial court or arbitration centre. Arbitration of international disputes is usually seated elsewhere.

data_protection.law: No comprehensive data protection law (as of early 2025); Electronic Evidence Act, 2010 is relevant
data_protection.summary: As of early 2025 Dominica had no comprehensive data protection statute and no data protection authority. The OECS began work in 2022 on harmonised data protection legislation for its members, but we have not confirmed that Dominica has enacted any of it. In practice, investigative work involving personal data rests on confidentiality obligations, common law privacy and breach of confidence principles, banking secrecy and AML confidentiality provisions, and the client's own home-jurisdiction rules, such as GDPR where a European controller is involved. The Electronic Evidence Act, 2010 governs whether electronic records are admissible. TDSC applies data minimisation and documented lawful purpose regardless.

investigator_regulation: We have not identified a dedicated licensing regime for private investigators in Dominica, nor a regulator that publishes a register of detective agencies. That does not make field activity unregulated. Criminal law, trespass, harassment and the confidentiality provisions of financial and AML legislation all limit what can lawfully be done. Records held by registered agents, banks and government departments are not open to private inquiry. Recording, surveillance and approaches to witnesses should be cleared with Dominican counsel first. In a small community, any local inquiry carries a real risk of the subject learning of it, which shapes how it is planned.
corporate_records: The Companies and Intellectual Property Office (CIPO), a department of the Ministry of National Security and Home Affairs, keeps registers of companies under the Companies Act, No. 21 of 1994, of business names and of external companies, and offers an E-Registry for filings. We have not confirmed a free public online search, and searches are often made through local agents or counsel. Beneficial ownership information is held by registered agents and financial institutions under the Money Laundering (Prevention) Act, 2011 framework and is not open to public inspection. Court records and land registry searches generally require attendance or local counsel.
anti_corruption: The Integrity in Public Office Act, No. 6 of 2003 established the Integrity Commission, which receives asset declarations from persons in public life and has functions relating to bribery and corrupt conduct. Anti-money laundering rules are set by the Money Laundering (Prevention) Act, No. 8 of 2011, as amended, and the Suppression of the Financing of Terrorism Act, 2003. The Financial Intelligence Unit operates under the Financial Intelligence Unit Act, No. 7 of 2011, and the Financial Services Unit supervises the non-bank financial sector.

matters.title: Due diligence on CBI passport holders
matters.text: Identity, reputation and source-of-wealth checks on individuals who hold Dominican citizenship by investment. These rely on records from their country of origin and residence, as well as Dominica, and test whether a second passport sits alongside undisclosed litigation, regulatory history or sanctions exposure.

matters.title: Real estate and hotel project review
matters.text: Background and track-record research on developers and promoters of CBI-approved hotel and real estate projects. This covers related entities, completion history, disputes and the people behind special-purpose vehicles that investors or lenders depend on.

matters.title: Legacy offshore entity tracing
matters.text: Following former international business companies and other Dominican vehicles after the 2021 repeal of the IBC regime. This means locating successor entities, registered agents and links to structures in other Caribbean and overseas jurisdictions, using lawful public and litigation sources.

matters.title: Asset tracing for enforcement
matters.text: Identifying land, vehicles, business interests and connected parties in Dominica to support enforcement of foreign judgments or awards. Searches are coordinated with Dominican counsel because registry access and recognition procedures run through the Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court.

matters.title: Reconstruction contract disputes
matters.text: Fact-finding and counterparty research for disputes over construction, supply and infrastructure contracts. Many of these are tied to rebuilding and resilience projects after Hurricane Maria in 2017 and are often funded or overseen by international partners.

practical.label: Currency
practical.value: East Caribbean dollar (XCD), pegged to the US dollar

practical.label: Business culture
practical.value: Small, relationship-driven market; introductions and discretion matter

practical.label: Document formalities
practical.value: Certified copies and notarisation commonly required; confirm with counsel

tdsc_approach: TDSC handles Dominica matters from Nashville. Most engagements start with a jurisdictional review: what is actually held in Dominica, what sits with registered agents or banks that cannot be reached without a court order, and what is better pursued in the subject's home or residence jurisdictions. We use lawful sources, including published court decisions, gazette notices, CIPO filings obtained through proper channels, media archives and international litigation records. Where on-island inquiries or record retrieval are needed, we coordinate qualified local professionals and work alongside the client's Dominican counsel, who advise on law. Because the community is small, we limit the number of people aware of an inquiry, keep personal data to what the stated purpose needs, and hold working files in our US systems under documented retention rules.

faqs.q: Can you confirm whether someone holds Dominican citizenship by investment?
faqs.a: Dominica does not publish a searchable list of CBI recipients, and we do not access government systems. We can assess the question indirectly through public sources, litigation records and documents the subject or counterparty provides, and we report how confident we are in what we find. Formal confirmation usually has to come from the individual or through a lawful process.

faqs.q: Are shareholder and beneficial owner details for Dominican companies public?
faqs.a: Generally not. CIPO holds incorporation records, but beneficial ownership information is kept by registered agents and financial institutions and is not open to public inspection. Regulators, the Financial Intelligence Unit, law enforcement and courts can obtain it. Private parties usually need a disclosure order sought through Dominican counsel, or need to rely on records in other jurisdictions.

We have not identified a specific licensing statute or public register for private investigators in Dominica. We do not treat that as a gap to exploit. Any local inquiry is scoped with Dominican counsel and carried out by qualified professionals within criminal, trespass and confidentiality law, with no pretexting and no attempts to obtain protected records.

faqs.q: How would a foreign judgment be enforced against assets in Dominica?
faqs.a: Enforcement is a question for Dominican counsel and depends on where the judgment came from and on applicable reciprocal enforcement legislation. Our role is to find assets and connected parties beforehand, such as land, business interests and vehicles, so that counsel can judge whether proceedings before the Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court are worthwhile.

faqs.q: Which court has the final word in Dominican cases?
faqs.a: Since March 2015 the Caribbean Court of Justice has been Dominica's final court of appeal, replacing the Privy Council. Below it sit the High Court and Court of Appeal of the Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court. CCJ and ECSC judgments are published, which makes them useful sources for background litigation research.
